common_name: Rush American Hazelnut (1917 J.F. Jones Selection, Foundation Parent of Modern Hybrid Hazels)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root plants in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rush is a historic named selection of native American hazelnut and needs a second, genetically distinct hazelnut planted within about 20 feet for wind pollination and reliable nut set.

directions: Rush was selected around 1917 by nurseryman J.F. Jones of Lancaster, Pennsylvania from an unusually prolific wild plant of native Corylus americana, and released under the clonal name 'Rush' for its heavy, reliable yields. Its greater historical significance lies in breeding: starting in 1919 Jones used Rush as the seed parent to cross with European hazelnut (Corylus avellana) clones including Barcelona, Cosford, Daviana, Italian Red, and Kentish Cob, producing the first American-European hybrid hazels; USDA breeder Clarence A. Reed and later programs continued using Rush as foundation breeding stock. The Rush resistance source has held up against Eastern Filbert Blight in the eastern US and Ontario since the 1940s, and its genes underlie a large share of modern EFB-resistant hybrid hazelnut breeding lines, including material behind the Rutgers New Jersey releases. Nuts are smaller than European hazelnut but flavorful and produced in dependable quantity even in cold climates, ripening in late summer to fall. Rush is not self-fertile and requires a second, genetically distinct hazelnut nearby for cross-pollination; it is more susceptible to hazelnut bud mite than some later selections. The shrub suckers to form a multi-stemmed thicket and can be grown directly as a durable native nut shrub or valued by breeders and collectors as a living link to the foundation of hybrid hazelnut breeding.
